newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech Deputy PM says import surcharge still needed.
newsitem.headline: Czech Deputy PM says import surcharge still needed.

text.p: Czech Deputy Prime Minister Josef Lux said on Tuesday he did not believe the recent depreciation of the crown would be enough to reverse the growth in the foreign trade deficit without the imposition of an import surcharge.

Lux told a news conference he believed the government would be forced to impose an import surcharge in the second half of this year, a move already advocated by Lux's Christian Democrats (KDU-CSL) in recent talks on an emergency economic package within the ruling coalition.
KDU proposed an immediate import surcharge as part of the government's austerity package agreed by the three coalition parties last week.
But the other partners in the centre-right coalition rejected the idea, agreeing however to take such a step in the second half of the year if necessary.

The centrist Christian Democrats are a junior party in the government coalition with the Civic Democratic Party (ODS) of Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus, and the pro-business Civic Democratic Alliance (ODA).

"We agreed that if (the coalition partners) are right and if it proves in a few months that trends have reversed, then there will be no reason to debate an import surcharge," Lux told a news conference.
"In case it does not prove to be, and I expect it, we agreed we would come back to this debate and that an import surcharge will be implemented," he said.

Following an attack by speculators on the crown which resulted in a roughly eight percent drop last week after the central bank was forced to float the currency, the government admitted mistakes in economic policies and agreed on a number of steps to help the ailing economy.

The cabinet's "short-term stabilisation programme" includes extensive government spending cuts leading to a balanced 1997 budget, support of the Czech National Bank's restrictive monetary policy and a freeze on growth in public sector wages.
The country's growing current account and trade deficits, along with a lack of restructuring and economic slowdown, have been cited as key causes in the recent attack on the currency.

The trade gap totalled 53.6 billion crowns in the first four months of 1997 after 39.6 billion in the same period of the previous year. Analysts forecasts before the crown's sharp drop put the full year trade deficit at between 180 to over 200 billion crowns after a 160.3 billion crown deficit in 1996.
